opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most underappreciated dynamics when people in the U.S. look at the Chinese AI ecosystem. There's a strong cultural and strategic instinct in China that if a technology is going to be foundational, you need to own it end to end. You don't want to be building your whole economy on top of something that someone else controls and could take away from you. And we've seen that play out with export controls on chips, so it's not a theoretical worry for them. It's something they've lived through.

So when you look at why so many Chinese companies (the big tech players like Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent, and then the startups like DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax) are each training their own models, part of it is commercial competition. But a big part of it is this sense that the model is now a core piece of infrastructure, like an operating system or a cloud platform. If you're a serious technology company, you don't want to rent your brain from someone else. That's different from a lot of Western enterprises, which are pretty comfortable just calling the OpenAI or Anthropic API and building on top.

What's interesting is how that connects to open weights. You might think an ownership mindset would push people toward keeping everything closed. But in China a lot of the leading labs have released really strong open-weight models. I think that comes from a few things. One, open-sourcing builds influence and an ecosystem around your model, globally and domestically. Two, it's a talent and reputation play. Researchers want to publish and have their work used. And three, for a lot of these companies the model isn't the only product. They make money elsewhere, so commoditizing the model layer doesn't hurt them the way it would hurt a pure model company.

From where I sit, working on open models in the U.S., this has been a bit of a wake-up call. For a while the best open-weight models in the world were coming out of China, and that has real consequences for who sets the standards, whose models people fine-tune, and whose values and defaults get baked into the ecosystem. So I'd say the ownership mindset is a big reason China has moved so fast. They decided early that this was technology they had to be able to build themselves, and they've invested accordingly. The question for the U.S. is whether we take open models as seriously from a strategic perspective, rather than leaving that space to others.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the best way to understand it is that for a lot of Chinese companies, building the model yourself isn't really optional in the way it sometimes feels optional for an American company. If you're in the US, you can sit on top of OpenAI or Anthropic or Google and feel pretty comfortable that the API will be there tomorrow. In China, that assumption just doesn't hold. You've got export controls on chips, you've got uncertainty about whether you'll have access to Western APIs at all, and you've got a government that has made pretty clear it wants domestic capability in this area. So the baseline mindset is: if we don't own the stack, we don't really have a business.

What's interesting to me is how that plays out culturally inside these labs. The people at DeepSeek, at Qwen, at Moonshot, Zhipu, and so on, they tend to talk about the model as the core asset, not a feature. In the US, I'd say a lot of companies are still debating whether they even want to be in the model business, because it's expensive and the frontier moves fast. In China, that debate is more or less settled. You train your own models, you release a lot of them, and you iterate publicly. The openness, with so many of these models coming out with open weights, is partly a strategy for distribution and recruiting and partly a reflection of the fact that they know they can't win on exclusivity against the biggest American labs, so they win on access and speed.

And I'd add that it's a very engineering-forward ownership mindset. The DeepSeek papers are a good example. They're not just saying "we trained a big model," they're showing you the infrastructure tricks, the efficiency work, the training details, because the constraint environment forces you to actually understand every layer of the system. When you can't just buy more H100s, you have to own the problem more deeply. So I think "ownership" there means something closer to mastery than to intellectual property. It's less about protecting the thing and more about being able to build the thing yourself, under constraint, repeatedly.

astra-6.text:
I think the mindset is that if AI is going to be a core technology for your business, you want to own the capability to build it. You don’t want your entire product roadmap to depend on somebody else’s API, pricing, or decisions about what you’re allowed to do.

And owning that capability means more than having the model weights. It means having a team that understands the data, the training process, and how to improve the model for your particular needs. Even if your model isn’t the best in the world on every benchmark, that expertise can be strategically valuable.

So I’d interpret it as a desire for technological independence and control. That isn’t unique to Chinese companies, but concerns about access to technology can make the motivation stronger. From that perspective, building your own model is an investment in being able to shape your future products.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a strong desire to own the core technology rather than build a business that depends on somebody else’s model. If you think AI is going to be an important part of your products, then relying entirely on an outside provider creates a dependency: they control the pricing, the capabilities, and the direction of development.

Building your own model gives you more control over those decisions, and it lets you develop the expertise internally. That doesn’t mean every company needs to train a frontier model from scratch. There’s a spectrum, from adapting open models to doing the whole training process yourself. But the underlying question is similar: how much of this technology do we need to understand and control to shape our own future?

I wouldn’t frame that as uniquely Chinese, though. You see the same motivation in American companies. The interesting distinction is how different companies weigh that ownership against the cost of building and maintaining the models.
